Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 61, verse 1:

(p-474)

Surat "As-Saff" (The Ranks)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾ It is narrated that they said, before they were commanded to fight (jihad): "If we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah, we would do them." So the verse on jihad was revealed, and some of them held back, so there was revealed:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 61, verse 2:

﴿O you who have believe, why do you say what you do not do?﴾, "لِمَ" (li-ma), is the lam of attribution (lam al-idafa), entering upon "ma" (ma), the interrogative, just as other prepositional particles entered upon it in your saying: "bima" (bi-ma), "fima" (fi-ma), "mimma" (min-ma), "amma" (an-ma), "ilamma" (ila-ma), and "alamma" (ala-ma). The alif was elided because "ma" and the lam (or other than it) became like one word, and it is very common in the speech of the one asking a question. The use of the original form has come rarely; he said:

؎ عَلاما قامَ يَشْتُمُنِي جَرِيرٌ؟!......................

Pausing (waqf) is on the addition of the silent ha' (ha' al-sakt), or on sukun (the quiescent vowel). And whoever uses sukun in connected speech (wasl), it is because he treats it as if it were in pause (waqf).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 61, verse 3:

﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.﴾

He intends by "kabura" (it is great) the expression of amazement (*ta'ajjub*), without using its verb form, as in his saying: "The blood-price of Kulayb's fang has become costly, its blood-wealth." [p. 475] The meaning of amazement is to magnify the matter in the hearts of the listeners, because amazement arises only from something outside its like. The verb is attributed to "an taqulu" (that you say), and "maqtan" (abhorrence) is put in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification). In this there is an indication that their saying what they do not do is pure abhorrence with no admixture. The meaning is: "Your saying what you do not do is great abhorrence in the sight of Allah." The word *maqt* was chosen because it is the most intense hatred. It is related from one of the *salaf* (early pious predecessors) that he was asked, "Narrate to us," and he said: "Do you order me to say what I do not do, and so hasten the wrath of Allah?!" Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed of what He loves, and said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 61, verse 4:

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks (ṣaffan)﴾, i.e., "standing in rows, themselves," (ṣāffīna anfusahum), a verbal noun (maṣdar) that has taken the place of a circumstantial state (ḥāl),

﴿as though they were a structure well-compacted (bunyānun marṣūṣ)﴾, adhering to one another. It has also been said that what is meant is the evenness of their intentions in fighting their enemy, so that they are, in the unity of their word, like a structure whose parts have been fitted tightly to one another. This too is a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 61, verse 5:

﴿Wa-idh﴾ (and when) is in the accusative case, governed by "udhkur" (remember),

﴿Qala Musa li-qawmihi: ya qawmi lima tu'dhunOnni﴾ (Moses said to his people: "O my people, why do you hurt me"), by denying the signs and by slandering me with what is not in me,

﴿wa-qad ta'lamuna﴾ (while you certainly know), is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: you hurt me while knowing with certain knowledge,

﴿anni rasulu Allahi ilaykum﴾ (that I am the Messenger of God to you). The consequence of your knowing this should be my reverence and honor, not that you hurt me.

﴿Falamma zaghu﴾ (So when they deviated), they inclined away from the truth,

﴿azagha Allahu qulubahum﴾ (God made their hearts deviate), from guidance. Or: when they abandoned His commands, He removed the light of faith from their hearts. Or: when they chose deviation, God made their hearts deviate, i.e., He forsook them and deprived them of the success of following the truth.

﴿wallahu la yahdi al-qawma al-fasiqin﴾ (And God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people), i.e., He does not guide those whom He knew in advance to be defiantly disobedient.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 61, verse 6:

﴿And when Jesus, the son of Mary, said: O Children of Israel,﴾, and he did not say "O my people" as Moses said, because he had no lineage among them that would make them his people,

﴿Indeed I am the Messenger of God to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah, and giving glad tidings of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad.﴾ That is: I was sent to you while confirming what preceded me of the Torah, and while giving glad tidings of a Messenger who will come after me. That is to say: my religion is the affirmation of the Books of God and of all His prophets, those who came before and those who came after. "Ba'di" (after me) is read by the people of the Hijaz, Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr, and this is the preference of al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, the grammarian) and Sibawayh. "Musaddiqan" (confirming) and "mubashshiran" (giving glad tidings) are in the accusative, governed by the sense of sending (irsal) contained in "Messenger."

﴿So when he came to them﴾, that is Jesus or Muhammad, upon both of them be blessings and peace,

﴿with clear proofs﴾, with miracles,

﴿they said: This is evident magic﴾, "sahir" (magic, as a noun in the form of "sahir"), read by Hamzah and Ali.

And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah while he is being invited to Islam? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people. [Qur'an 61:7]

And who among people is more unjust than one whom his Lord calls, through the tongue of His Prophet, to Islam, in which lies the happiness of both abodes, so that instead of responding to it he makes the fabrication of a lie against Allah his response, by saying of His speech, which is the calling of His servants to the truth: "This is sorcery." Sorcery is a lie and deception.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 61, verse 8:

﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾. This is a mockery of them in their desire to nullify Islam, by their saying about the Qur'an: "This is sorcery." Their condition is depicted as that of one who blows into the light of the sun with his mouth in order to extinguish it. The object is omitted, and the lam is for causation (ta'lil), and the estimated reading is: "They desire falsehood, so that they may extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, i.e., with their speech,

﴿But Allah will complete His light﴾. Makki, Hamza, Ali and Hafs read "mutimmu nurihi" (with the genitive of the pronoun), while others read "mutimmun nurahu" (with the accusative), i.e., the Truth will be completed, and its proclaimer will reach its goal,

﴿although the disbelievers dislike it﴾.

He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth — that is, the upright religion (al-milla al-hanifiyya),

﴿that He may make it prevail﴾, that is, to make it exalted,

﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾, over all the religions that oppose it. By my life, He has indeed done so: no religion remains except that it is overcome and subdued by the religion of Islam. And it is related from Mujahid: "When ʿIsa (Jesus) descends, there will be nothing on earth but the religion of Islam,"

﴿even though the polytheists dislike it﴾.

Ye who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?

"تُنَجِّيكُمْ" (tunajjīkum), read by al-Shāmī (Ibn ʿĀmir al-Shāmī).

(p-477) "Tu'minūn" (you believe) is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), as if they had said: "How shall we act?" So he said: "Tu'minūn," which, according to Sibawayh, has the meaning of the imperative "Āminū" (believe!). This is why it is answered with His words: "He will forgive you your sins." This is also indicated by the reading of Ibn Mas'ūd: "Āminū bi-Llāh wa-rasūlihi wa-jāhidū" (believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive). It was expressed in the form of a statement to signify the obligation of compliance, as if he had already complied, so He reports of a faith and a struggle that exist,

"In Allah and His Messenger, and you strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That" — i.e., what has been mentioned of faith and striving —

"is better for you" — than your wealth and your lives —

"if you knew" — that it is better for you. It would be better for you at that time, because when you know that and believe in it, you will love faith and striving more than you love your wealth and your lives, and so you will be saved and you will prosper.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 61, verse 12:

﴿He will forgive you your sins and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in Gardens of Eden.﴾ Meaning: a dwelling and an everlasting abode. It is said: "'adana bil-makan" (ʿadana bi-l-makān), meaning he settled in the place, when he stayed in it. So it is said.

﴿That is the great triumph.﴾

And another [favour] that you love: in addition to this blessing mentioned, namely forgiveness and reward in the Hereafter, there is for you another blessing in this world, which is beloved to you. Then he explained it with His words: **﴿help from Allah and a near victory﴾**, i.e., imminent. This is the conquest of Mecca and victory over Quraysh, or the conquest of Persia and Rome. In "**تُحِبُّونَها**" (you love it) there is a degree of rebuke for loving what is immediate. The author of al-Kashshaf (Sahib al-Kashshaf, al-Zamakhshari) said: "Its meaning is: shall I guide you to a trade that will save you, and to another trade that you love?" Then he said: "**نَصْرٌ**" (help), meaning: "it is help."

**﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾**: this is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "**تُؤْمِنُونَ**" (you believe), because it carries the meaning of a command, as if it were said: "Believe and strive, and Allah will make you firm and help you; and give good tidings, O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to the believers of that." It was also said: it is a conjunction upon "**قُلْ**" (say), intended before "**﴿O you who believe, shall I guide you to a bargain?﴾**" [al-Saff: 10].

O you who believe, be helpers of Allah. That is, helpers of His religion. "Ansaran lillah" is read by Ibn Kathir of Hijaz (Hijazi) and Abu Amr.

﴿As Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples (al-ḥawāriyyūn), "Who are my helpers toward Allah?"﴾ Its outward meaning is a comparison between their being helpers and Jesus's words, "Who are my helpers toward Allah?" But it is to be understood in terms of meaning: "Be helpers of Allah just as the disciples were helpers of Jesus when he said to them, 'Who are my helpers toward Allah?'" Its meaning is "Who is my army, heading toward supporting Allah?" so that it matches the disciples' reply, which is His saying: ﴿The disciples said, "We are helpers of Allah."﴾ That is, we are those who support Allah. The meaning of "Who are my helpers?" is: who are the helpers who are devoted to me and who will be with me in supporting Allah? "Al-ḥawāriyyūn" are his chosen ones, the first to believe in him, and they were twelve men. "Ḥawārī al-rajul" means a man's chosen friend and pure companion, from "al-ḥawar," which is pure white. It was said that they were launderers who whiten clothes, that is, they made them white.

﴿Then a group of the Children of Israel believed﴾ in Jesus.

﴿And a group disbelieved﴾ in him.

﴿So We strengthened those who believed against their enemy﴾, that is, We strengthened their believers against their disbelievers.

﴿So they became victorious﴾, that is, they prevailed over them.
